metaTitle: Where Do Bed Bugs Hide? Mattress Seams First
metaDescription: Bed bugs hide in mattress seams, box springs, bed frames and headboards first, then furniture, walls and luggage. See how to inspect a room.
h1: Where Do Bed Bugs Hide? Hiding Places From the Mattress Outward
dek: The spots bed bugs use, ordered by how close they are to where you sleep, how far the bugs travel to feed, and how to inspect a bedroom or hotel room.
excerpt: Bed bugs hide in mattress seams, box springs, headboards and bed frames first. Here is how far they roam, when they feed and how to inspect a bedroom or hotel room.

quickAnswer.lead: **Bed bugs hide closest to where people sleep: in the seams, piping and tags of the mattress and box spring, and in cracks of the bed frame and headboard.** In heavier infestations they spread to furniture, baseboards, outlets and belongings. [The EPA](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) says they readily travel 5 to 20 feet from their hiding places to feed.
bullets: The EPA's rule of thumb is that any crack that will hold a credit card could hide a bed bug.
Bed bugs readily travel 5 to 20 feet from established hiding places to feed, according to the EPA.
Adults are about 3/16 inch long, and the largest share of any population is always immature bugs that are smaller still.
Bed bugs are active mainly at night, but a hungry bug may feed during the day, per the University of Kentucky.
Virginia Tech's guide says bed bugs feed about every 5 to 7 days when a host is present and spend the other days digesting.

body.text: Where do bed bugs hide?

Bed bugs hide as close to the people they feed on as they can, so the first places to look are the piping, seams and tags of the mattress and box spring and the cracks in the bed frame and headboard. That is the list [the EPA's guide to finding bed bugs](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) gives for the usual hiding places near beds. The [University of Kentucky's bed bug fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef636) makes the same point in a line: bed bugs prefer to hide close to where they feed.

The EPA adds that in heavily infested rooms they also turn up in the seams of chairs and couches, between cushions, in curtain folds, in drawer joints, in electrical outlets, under loose wallpaper and wall hangings, at ceiling-wall junctions and in screw heads.

The sources list hiding places rather than ranking them by how often bugs are found, so the table below orders them by distance from the bed. That order is a reading of the sources, not a measured ranking. For the wider picture of how infestations start, spread and end, see [the complete bed bug reference](/learn/bed-bugs).

body.text: Which parts of the bed do bed bugs hide in first?

The mattress and box spring come first, followed by the frame and headboard. The University of Kentucky lists mattress seams, folds and crevices, the upper seams and underside of the box spring, and bed frames and headboards as the primary locations, along with items stored under the bed.
Mattress piping, seams and tags

Check every seam and fold around the mattress, plus the tag. Virginia Tech entomologist Dini Miller's guide, [How to Identify a Bed Bug Infestation](https://www.vdacs.virginia.gov/pdf/bb-identify1.pdf), names the mattress seams, the tufts and the area under the mattress tags as places where bed bugs gather in groups, and lists the seams and tag among the places fecal spots are most likely to appear when an infestation is small. The EPA adds rusty or reddish stains on sheets and mattresses, which come from bugs that were crushed. A separate guide shows [what bed bug signs on a mattress look like and what to do about them](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress).

body.text: The box spring

The sources name several box spring hiding places. Virginia Tech lists fecal spots on the wood frame of the box spring, aggregations along wood creases in box springs and bed frames, and aggregations where the box spring fabric is stapled to the wood frame. Kentucky points to the upper seams and the underside.
Bed frame and headboard

The frame and the headboard offer cracks, joints and screw holes. The EPA names cracks on the bed frame and headboard, and Virginia Tech adds the holes for set-in screws and the space behind the headboard, which it also lists as a place to find shed skins. Kentucky says a thorough inspection requires dismantling the bed and standing its components on edge.

body.needed: Photo of the back of a wooden headboard lit by a flashlight beam, showing a cluster of dark spots and a few bed bugs in a joint near a screw hole

body.text: Do bed bugs hide in nightstands, dressers and other furniture?

Yes. Kentucky names nightstands, dressers and the crevices of wooden furniture, plus the seams and fabric folds of upholstered chairs, recliners and sofas. The EPA lists drawer joints and the spaces between cushions among the places bugs spread to in a heavily infested room. Items stored under the bed also appear on the Kentucky list, which is a reason to pull them out and check them early.

None of the sources gives a figure for how often each kind of furniture is occupied, so treat bedside furniture and sofas as the next stops after the bed and frame. If a bug you find on furniture does not look right, [a comparison of the insects most often mistaken for bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs) covers carpet beetles, bat bugs and other look-alikes.
Can bed bugs hide in walls, baseboards and outlets?

Yes, particularly once a population has grown. Kentucky lists baseboards and carpet edges, the perimeter of wall-to-wall carpeting, cracks in wood molding, ceiling-wall junctions, and the spaces behind pictures, mirrors, outlets and switch plates. The EPA adds electrical outlets, loose wallpaper, wall hangings and screw heads. Virginia Tech's list of aggregation sites includes behind loose wallpaper, behind chipped paint, behind baseboards, inside baseboard heaters and under the base of an air conditioner.

Wall and ceiling clusters are easy to misread. Dini Miller's guide includes a photograph of an apartment ceiling that first looked like mold or mildew from a moisture problem upstairs; on closer inspection it was many bed bug aggregations, and the black material was fecal spotting. If a dark patch on a ceiling or wall edge looks like mold, check it closely for bugs, skins and tiny eggs before deciding what it is.
Walls and ceilings also serve as routes. According to Kentucky, bed bugs can crawl from room to room, or from floor to floor, through cracks and openings in walls, floors and ceilings.
How far do bed bugs travel from their hiding places?

The EPA says bed bugs will readily travel 5 to 20 feet from established hiding places to feed. The sources used here give no maximum distance. Kentucky says bed bugs crawl rapidly over floors, walls, ceilings and other surfaces but cannot fly or jump, and that they will crawl longer distances in search of a meal when they have to, even though they prefer to hide close to where they feed.
By that measure, a baseboard or outlet across a room can still be within range of the bed, which is why an inspection does not stop at the mattress.
When do bed bugs come out of hiding?

Mostly at night. Kentucky says bed bugs are active mainly at night and usually bite people while they are sleeping, though a hungry bug may also feed during the day. A meal does not take long: the EPA gives 3 to 12 minutes, and Kentucky says engorgement takes about 3 to 10 minutes.

Between meals the bugs are out of sight. Virginia Tech's guide says bed bugs feed about every 5 to 7 days when a host is present and spend the days in between digesting. They excrete part of each meal as semi-liquid waste, deposited wherever they go after feeding, which dries into the black spots described below. Those spots are often found in groups of 10 or more, though a bug that was only passing through may leave one or two.

Size is the other reason they go unseen. An unfed adult is about 3/16 inch long and can look like a flat disc, and Virginia Tech says the largest share of any bed bug population is always immature. Immature bugs are smaller than adults and translucent whitish-yellow, and the youngest nymphs are hard to see unless they are moving or have just fed. [How to recognize each life stage](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like) is covered in its own guide, and [what the small black specks really are](/blog/black-bed-bugs) in another.
How small a gap can a bed bug squeeze into?

A crack that will hold a credit card is enough. That is the EPA's yardstick: if a gap is wide enough for a credit card, it could hide a bed bug. It is why the sources keep pointing to seams, joints, screw heads and the gaps behind trim rather than flat surfaces.

Eggs are tinier still. The EPA puts eggs at about 1 millimeter (roughly 1/25 inch), and Virginia Tech compares an egg to the head of a pin and says eggs are pearl-white with obvious eyespots once they are more than 5 days old. Kentucky says eggs hatch in about a week at room temperature.
Do bed bugs hide in luggage, clothing and belongings?

Yes, and that is how they get into a home. Kentucky says bed bugs are easily transported into dwellings on luggage, clothing, beds, furniture and belongings. Virginia Tech's guide says bed bugs have to be brought into a home, for example in luggage after a trip or on a piece of used furniture.

Once inside, belongings become hiding places. Virginia Tech lists books, stuffed animals and picture frames, plus the framing under a closet bar and the interior frame of closet doors. Kentucky adds closet clutter, clothing and book bindings, and also names clocks, phones, televisions and smoke detectors.

body.title: Bites are a poor way to find the hiding place
body.text: Virginia Tech says bite reactions vary so much from person to person that bites are not a good way to diagnose an infestation. Someone bitten while traveling may not react for several days, and Kentucky reports that about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly.
How do you inspect a bedroom for bed bugs?

Start with the bed and work outward, looking for evidence as well as live bugs. Bites alone cannot confirm anything ([what bed bug bites look like and how to tell for sure](/blog/bed-bug-bites) explains why), so look for the physical signs. A flashlight helps, according to Kentucky, because many hiding places are dim. The EPA's list of signs covers rusty or reddish stains on sheets and mattresses, dark spots about the size of a bullet point, eggs and eggshells, shed skins, and the live bugs themselves.

body.text: Dini Miller's guide gives a quick test for black spots that could be cockroach droppings: bed bug spots feel smooth because they are dried blood, while German cockroach droppings feel granular. It also advises looking for shed skins or hatched eggs nearby. A longer guide covers [what bed bug droppings and stains look like, and the marks they get confused with](/blog/bed-bug-stains-poop-droppings-canada).

items: Strip the bed and look over the sheets and mattress cover for rusty stains, dark spots and bugs in the folds.
Work all the way around the mattress, checking the piping, seams, tufts and tag.
Lift the mattress off and inspect the box spring: the upper seams, the underside, creases in the wood and the staples that hold the fabric to the frame.
Take the frame apart if you can, stand the pieces on edge, and check the joints, cracks and screw holes, then look behind the headboard.
Open the nightstand and dresser drawers and check the joints and crevices, and pull out anything stored under the bed.
Follow the room's edges: baseboards, carpet edges, ceiling-wall junctions, outlets and switch plates, and the backs of pictures and mirrors.
Finish with the sofa and chair seams, the curtain folds and pleats near the rod, the closet door frames and the belongings stacked nearby.

body.text: Tools that help

items: **Flashlight.** Kentucky recommends one for dimly lit areas.
**Interceptor cups.** Kentucky describes dish-shaped traps placed under furniture legs, and a separate guide covers [how to read an interceptor trap](/blog/bed-bug-interceptor-traps-canada).
**A credit card as a gauge.** The EPA uses it to show which gaps are large enough to hide a bug.
**Trained dogs.** Kentucky notes that some companies use specially trained canines to find bed bugs.

body.text: How do you check a hotel room for bed bugs?

Use the same bed-outward order, and spend most of your time on the bed and headboard. The sources behind this page describe where bed bugs hide and do not give a hotel-specific checklist, so these steps apply their hiding-place lists to a hotel room.

items: **Mattress.** Pull back the sheets and check the piping, seams and tag at the corners.
**Headboard and frame.** Look at the headboard, its joints and screw holes and, where you can see it, the gap behind it.
**Bedside furniture.** Check the nightstand and its drawer joints, and the wall and outlets nearest the bed.
**Curtains and room edges.** Look at the pleats near the curtain rod, the baseboards and the ceiling-wall junction near the bed.
**Your own belongings.** Kentucky and Virginia Tech both name luggage as a way bed bugs travel into a home, so inspect bags and clothing when you unpack.

body.text: Finding nothing is not proof of nothing. Virginia Tech says that in a new infestation, a hotel room for example, bed bug evidence may be very hard to find, but because most of a population is immature there is always a chance of finding cast skins. It also notes that a person bitten while traveling may not react for several days, and that bites noticed after getting home do not mean the home is infested.
What should you do after finding bed bug hiding places?

Confirm what you found before treating anything. If the bug or the specks might be something else, [the look-alike guide](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs) helps you rule things out, and if what you found is an empty shell, [a guide to bed bug shells, casings and shed skins](/blog/bed-bug-shells-casings-shed-skins-canada) covers whether it still means an active problem. Once the bugs are confirmed, [the step-by-step plan to get rid of bed bugs](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs) explains what to do with the bed, the room and your belongings.

faqs.question: Can bed bugs live inside a mattress?
faqs.answer: They hide in the mattress seams, folds, piping, tufts and under the tag. The University of Kentucky lists mattress seams, folds and crevices as primary locations, and Virginia Tech's guide names the seams, tufts and tag area as places bugs gather in groups. The EPA lists piping, seams and tags for both the mattress and the box spring.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs come out during the day?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, though mainly they feed at night. The University of Kentucky says bed bugs are active mainly at night and usually bite people while they sleep, but a hungry bug may also feed during the day. Virginia Tech says bed bugs feed about every 5 to 7 days when a host is present and spend the days between meals digesting.

faqs.question: Can bed bugs hide in walls?
faqs.answer: They use the cracks and fixtures in and around walls. The EPA lists outlets, loose wallpaper, wall hangings, ceiling-wall junctions and screw heads. The University of Kentucky says they can crawl from room to room or floor to floor through cracks and openings in walls, floors and ceilings. Virginia Tech also lists baseboard heaters, chipped paint and the area behind baseboards.

faqs.question: How small a space can bed bugs fit into?
faqs.answer: Any gap that will hold a credit card, according to the EPA, which says that if a crack will hold one it could hide a bed bug. An unfed adult is about 3/16 inch long and can look like a flat disc, per Virginia Tech, which is why seams, joints, screw holes and the space behind trim all count as hiding places.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs hide in clothes and luggage?
faqs.answer: Yes. The University of Kentucky says bed bugs are easily transported into dwellings on luggage, clothing, beds, furniture and belongings, and Virginia Tech's guide describes bed bugs arriving in luggage after a trip or on used furniture. Inside a home, Kentucky also names closet clutter and clothing, and Virginia Tech lists books, stuffed animals and picture frames.

faqs.question: Can you have bed bugs without any bite marks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Virginia Tech says bite reactions vary so much that a person may not react at all, which can let an infestation go unnoticed until the population grows enough for the bugs to be seen. The University of Kentucky says about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly. Looking for spots, skins and eggs is more reliable than relying on bites.
